title: Navaratri: Rama wakes the Goddess
hookLine: before his last battle Rama wakes the Goddess out of season, and offers his own eye when one lotus goes missing
carry: shakti first: even rama asked the mother
last: BHAKTI: GOD WALKS TOWARD YOU TOO.

lines: WAKING THE GODDESS OUT OF SEASON.
cards: Rama has an army, a bridge across the sea, and Hanuman. Sita is across the water in Lanka. And Ravana still can't be beaten.

In the Bengali telling of the Ramayana, by the poet Krittivasa, Rama sees he can't win alone. He needs the Goddess. But it's autumn, and in the old reckoning this is the gods' night, their half of the year for sleeping.
So Rama does what no one had done before. He wakes the Goddess out of season.

teach.b: It's called akal bodhan, the untimely awakening. Rama sets up an image of Durga and worships her with everything he has.
For the last offering he needs a hundred and eight blue lotuses, and Hanuman flies off and brings them.

teach.h: ONE IS MISSING. HE OFFERS HIS EYE.
teach.b: Rama offers them one by one, a prayer with each. At the very end, his hand finds nothing. One lotus is missing.
In the telling, the Goddess herself has hidden it, to test him. And Rama remembers what people call him: the lotus-eyed one. He takes up an arrow to offer one of his own eyes as the last lotus.
Before he can, Durga appears, stops his hand, and blesses him. Then the war, and Ravana falls; many Hindus remember his fall on the tenth day.

teach.h: TWO VICTORIES ON THE TENTH DAY.
teach.b: That's why Bengal keeps its great Durga Puja in autumn, and why the tenth day, Vijayadashami, holds two victories: Durga's over the buffalo demon, and Rama's over Ravana. Now the teaching.
For many Hindus, Rama is God himself, born as a prince.

teach.h: EVEN GOD BOWS TO THE GODDESS.
teach.b: And even he bows to the Goddess before the battle. Many Hindus, especially those who worship the Goddess, teach that Shakti, the Mother's power, is what makes every action possible, even God's.
So before the hard thing, you go to her.
That's what the nine nights are for many families: nine forms of the Goddess, the Navadurga, one honored each night, from Shailaputri, daughter of the mountain, to Siddhidatri, giver of perfection.
And notice what Rama offered. Not gold. Himself, holding nothing back.

teach.h: SHAKTI FIRST: EVEN RAMA ASKED THE MOTHER.
teach.b: Shakti first: even Rama asked the Mother.

how: Hindus keep Navaratri in many regional ways: honoring a form of the Goddess each night (the Navadurga), garba dancing in Gujarat, Durga Puja in Bengal, golu dolls in the south, and Ramlila plays in the north ending on Dussehra, when effigies of Ravana are burned.

that's the Bengali telling by Krittivasa; it's why Bengal keeps Durga Puja in autumn.
Durga stopped Rama before he could offer his eye
she appeared, stopped his hand and blessed him.
Rama is God, so he didn't need anyone's help
in the telling even Rama bows to the Goddess first: Shakti makes every action possible.

games.q: you're Rama. one of the 108 lotuses is missing, and the worship isn't finished. what do you do?
o: offer one of your own eyes: they call you the lotus-eyed.
send Hanuman back and start again tomorrow.
games.why: he holds nothing back, and Durga stops his hand and blesses him. shakti first: even Rama asked the Mother.

practice: Name one hard thing coming up this week. If you pray, light a lamp or picture one, and say Jai Mata Di, or a Durga prayer you know, and ask the Mother for strength before you start, the way Rama did.
If you don't pray, name the hard thing, then name one person whose strength you'd borrow for it. Three slow breaths, then rest.

wordCard.voice: Navaratri. Nine nights of the Goddess, and in Bengal's telling, the autumn Rama woke her out of season.

orig.note: Bengali: the untimely awakening, Rama's autumn worship of Durga.

carryVoice: Your line: shakti first: even rama asked the mother. Before the hard thing, go to the Goddess. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Krittivasi Ramayana, Lanka Kanda (Rama's akal bodhan of Durga; the 108 blue lotuses; the offered eye)
Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda (the Aditya Hridayam, taught to Rama by Agastya before the last battle)
Navadurga (the nine forms; listed in later devotional texts such as the Devi Kavacha)
Navaratri regional observance (Durga Puja in autumn, garba, golu, Ramlila and Dussehra)
